📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

If you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a upcoming phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

During the launch presentation, Xiaomi emphasized that its new privacy display wasn’t just a copy of “other privacy displays.” Rather, they created an entirely new subpixel layout called HyperRGB 2.0 that delivers far higher resolution and brightness output than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. You can also enable and disable the privacy display feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series with a click of the new AI button on the left side of the phone. Functionally, Xiaomi’s privacy display looks nearly identical to Samsung’s, including the ability to have specific apps use it.

Both models feature identical specs, including the privacy display and cameras, with the exception of the screen size, battery capacity, and charging speed. Here are the differences:.

Recent findings suggest that the 120Hz LTPO display is bordered by a 0.99mm bezel, the smallest in the industry so far, 4,000-nit peak brightness, and TÜV Rheinland Triple Eye Care Certification, including a 2160Hz PWM dimming rate. Inside the phone is a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor with a 3D IceLoop cooling system, and each model’s silicon-carbon battery includes 28% silicon content.

On the back is a pair of 200MP cameras, including a 1/1.28-inch main sensor and a 1/1.56-inch periscope telephoto sensor. These are massive sensors, especially compared to the 1/3.94″ and 1/2.52″ telephoto sensors in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Despite their size, Xiaomi packs them onto the back in an island with fully flat glass — no protruding camera lenses!

That island on the back isn’t just for cameras, though. It also packs in a 120Hz LTPO M11 OLED panel with 4,000-nit peak brightness for ultra-high-quality selfies and group shots, plus support for notifications and apps. Xiaomi created a latest GenAI Apps feature that lets you create your own apps on the back display, plus official support for several popular apps like Google Maps, Spotify, and more.

Industry observers note that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series ships with HyperOS 4 (Android 17) and includes 3 months of Google AI Pro, plus 5TB of Google Cloud storage. The Xiaomi 18 Pro retails for €1399 for the model with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, or €1599 for 12GB/512GB. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at €1599 for 12GB/256GB, €1799 for 12GB/512GB, and a 16GB/1TB model will be available soon for €2099.

It has been revealed that some retailers also sell a bundle that includes the Official silicone magnetic case, which usually retails for €39, as well as the Magnetic Remote Stand, which retails for €69. That remote stand functions as a MagSafe-style stand and remote, giving you camera shutter functionality and a scrolling feature.

How Anthropic believes branding will shape its post-IPO future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image.
  • Investors are fundamentally betting on the technology underpinning Anthropic’s products and business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image. ANT priced at $83 a share, above expectations, making it the biggest IPO of all time, worth a staggering $1.5 trillion; it finished its first trading day at $97.17. Investors are fundamentally betting on the technology underpinning Anthropic’s products and business. But in this case, it’s easy to overlook the importance of another factor that’s played a major role in the company’s remarkable rise: strong brand optics. Anthropic itself makes that case in its S-1 form, which gave investors a glimpse into the company’s thinking before its IPO. Tellingly, the word “brand” appears 63 times. Admittedly, the S-1 is a book-length document covering many topics. But the filing reveals a company that recognizes how much branding has mattered in a razor-competitive category like AI—and how much it will matter in the future. Many of Anthropic’s rivals have launched on the backs of widely known brands or brand ecosystems: Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Muse, Elon Musk’s Grok, Microsoft’s Copilot. OpenAI became a household name thanks to the surprise popularity of its ChatGPT product, and an avalanche of publicity. Anthropic, by contrast, didn’t even exist until a few years ago, when a group broke away from OpenAI to found what was then an upstart rival. With a story specifically touting ethical responsibility and social trust, it leaned on a brand-forward identity from the start. With notable exceptions—Apple especially—tech companies often treat branding as a squishy afterthought. Innovation and word of mouth, the thinking goes, drive success, not a promoted public image. Anthropic, no doubt, attributes its rapidly growing profile to its flagship chatbot, Claude, and other products establishing it as a world-class AI lab with enormous upside potential (and similarly extreme risks). [Photo: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images] But it’s worth unpacking what that filing had to say on the subject of growth. It argues that even a category-leading product depends on brand reputation, and offers insight into how Anthropic will pursue its branding goals after the IPO. Building on its founding proposition as the AI company with a conscience, Anthropic seeks to cement an image that commingles efficiency and trust, leveraging individual connection with its products to fuel enterprise growth. For starters, Anthropic reports that its annual ad spending spiked from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million last year, and is expected to keep growing in 2026. (Notably, Anthropic advertised during the Super Bowl this year, poking at OpenAI for incorporating ads into its chat results.) That may not sound like much for a company that reported $33 billion in revenue through the first nine months of 2026, but it’s clear that its brand strategy isn’t just a gloss, and in fact will help drive growth. “The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive,” the filing explains. “If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers.” More specifically, Anthropic positions brand building as a way to become a recognizable, deliberately chosen collaborator to what it dubs “prosumers.” These individuals pay for AI tools to perform knowledge work and their personal product preferences can influence organizational purchasing like, say, bringing Claude into their workplaces. The filing doesn’t quite suggest that Anthropic thinks models are becoming commodities, or that branding will ultimately matter more than performance. But in effect, it argues that in an increasingly competitive market, the brand is going to matter a lot to consumers (or prosumers) who see rival products as somewhat interchangeable, and find it easy to jump from one to another. [Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images] And maybe more to the point: Many others see AI as a problem, spawning controversial data centers and threatening jobs. As the S-1 cautions, Anthropic’s brand must also contend with “broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct.”  The period just before Anthropic’s IPO was a rough stretch for the industry overall. It featured the Jensen Huang scandal at AI mainstay Nvidia, multiple air traffic and Internet failures that sparked (seemingly evidence-less) conspiracy theories centered on AI, and a handy New York Post quiz about surviving an “AI apocalypse.” Thus Anthropic has been at pains to distinguish itself as the cautious and thoughtful AI company, clashing with the Pentagon about military uses of its technology, claiming to want more regulation, keeping advertising out of its products—and going public as a public benefit corporation, a structure meant to prod leadership to think beyond profits. Not everyone is convinced. Critics accuse Anthropic leadership of having a “savior complex.” But it does seem remarkable that its IPO was such a roaring success despite a terrible stretch for the sector overall. The stock market measures investor sentiment, which is not quite the same as brand reputation—but also not totally unrelated. Anthropic’s brand may have aided its IPO’s success. And that success is certainly good for the brand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, like millions of other Americans, I was stuck at an airport on the infamous Friday the 13th in November when air traffic in the U.S. came to a halt. From where I sat at Fort Lauderdale airport, the panic was obvious. Crowds overflowed at gates. Hotel rooms disappeared swiftly. I got one of the last ones available in the city. It was chaos. That’s what happens when big networks go down: chaos. And it’s only just beginning unless organizations fix how they change their network infrastructures. Of course, the ground stop would have made news by itself. But what really got people talking was that it was one of a series of major outages that occurred over just a few days’ time. Shortly before the ground stop, a Microsoft Outlook outage left businesses unable to send email. Our company had contracts held up by it. And on Monday, November 16, customers at several major banks found they couldn’t reach their accounts. Email, air travel, banking—three essential elements of the American economy, not to mention people’s daily lives—crashed in the span of just three business days. Suddenly, people who don’t know a router from a switch were talking about network infrastructure. Conspiracy theories multiplied on social media and in the dark corners of the internet. I spend my working life close to the networks behind failures like these, and I can say with complete confidence that there is no conspiracy here. The root cause of all the outages might sound less satisfying than a complex conspiracy theory, but it is daunting nonetheless: The infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change always brings risk. When organizations fail to manage changes in their network infrastructure, the result, as we all saw last week, can be chaos. It almost always starts with a change The issue at the root of network outages is almost always change. Based on what we know at this point, change was at the root of the air traffic control failure. The network that carries communications between the major air traffic control centers is decades old and in the middle of a long modernization, which involves moving from legacy protocols and transmission to modern fiber and latest equipment. At one step of that transition, when new network devices were introduced, something went wrong. A misconfiguration or a misbehaving device sent traffic into the network that other devices couldn’t handle. Those devices began to fail, and the failure cascaded. Shortly after, the rush to find a hotel room began. The Outlook outage had the same origin: configuration changes, unintended consequences, knock-on failures. Some of the triggering configurations were already months old and sat quietly until a condition in the network finally exposed them. Why can’t networks just heal themselves? So, why do these outages occur? Networks are supposed to route around damage. In theory, they should. But in practice, change can shake up a network infrastructure in unpredictable ways. A network is, by definition, a set of interacting systems. Change one element and you change how its neighbors behave, and how their neighbors behave after that. Change is necessary. Unfortunately, it’s not always good, and when it’s bad it just gets worse as it travels through the network infrastructure. That’s why the teams who run critical networks practice serious discipline before a change: pre-change testing, a mapped-out plan for every step, a rollback plan. I’m confident the people involved last week did all of that. But the interconnections inside a large network are so vast that no team can test for every eventuality. That’s not carelessness. It’s the nature of complex, interconnected systems. It could happen to even the most prepared team. Redundancy helps, and these networks have layers of it. But redundancy does not remove complexity. In some ways, it adds to it. Why recovery takes so long So if a change caused the problem, the simple solution is to undo the change. But that’s not easy to do because the same interconnectedness that caused the failure makes it hard to reverse. A problem becomes exponentially more difficult to fix as it cascades through the network infrastructure and tangles itself into a complex web of systems. Here’s what has to happen for a team to fix an issue related to change: The team has to diagnose it. When effects cascade across the network, often it’s not obvious which change caused which symptom. This is where visibility becomes critical. You can’t fix what you can’t see. An accurate picture of the network, what’s connected to what, how each element should be configured, and what is happening right now can make the difference between a fast fix and one that takes many times longer while the team works in the dark. The team has to remediate, and rollback is just the start. By the time the team finds a cause, the problem has usually triggered other failures. Elements of the network infrastructure have to talk to one another again before the network works as it should. That process often has to happen in a careful order so the applications on top return cleanly. Microsoft’s team reportedly spent days painstakingly rebuilding its environment to avoid further knock-on effects. The team has to regain confidence that the problem won’t come straight back. The initial fix doesn’t always work. And when lives depend on the answer, caution is always the right call. I compare this process to heart surgery on a global stage. Teams get it right 99.99% of the time, but almost nobody notices. Their effort is monumental and continuous but largely anonymous. But when there is an outage, they are doing delicate, high-stakes work while the public watches the departure boards. Get used to network outages However, we’re about to hear a lot more about these teams because the rate of change in our infrastructure is rapidly accelerating. There are three reasons why: Decades-old systems are hitting their limits and must be modernized, as is the case with air traffic control. Modernization requires change, and change always involves risk. AI is putting new demands on networks. Agents and AI-powered applications are doing real work, and that work runs over infrastructure that can’t adequately carry it without growth and adaptation. AI brings a whole new set of security implications. This reason is the most urgent of the three. In my industry, we talk about the “patchpocalypse.” AI is helping uncover vulnerabilities faster than ever, some of which have been hidden for years or even decades. The time between discovery and exploitation has shrunk from a quarter or a year to mere hours. Every patch is a change to the network, and every change carries risk. Put all of those factors together, and you get infrastructure that’s 30 or 40 years out of date and needs to change almost immediately. The networks themselves aren’t necessarily more fragile, but their criticality, complexity, and necessity for change are all growing faster than teams and funding can keep up. Everything is going to feel shaky for a while. Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

It has been revealed that the agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you strategy to run an agent on local hardware.

Industry observers note that openClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

According to recent reports, this article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

Industry observers note that the Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

Industry observers note that the extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:.

According to recent reports, on the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

Sources indicate that openClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

According to recent reports, the first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:.

The next requests were much faster:.

In a recent development, reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

It has been revealed that the speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the newly introduced tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

According to recent reports, ollama's documentation indicates models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

Recent findings suggest that A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

Industry observers note that an embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:.

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

The rest of the stack was light:.

It has been revealed that what this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:.

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:.

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

It has been revealed that in this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

It has been revealed that every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Sources indicate that yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly mentioned its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas.
  • In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas.
  • According to recent reports, instead of a plastic toy, the chain is offering free pairs of ugly Christmas socks with every purchase of its Home Alone-themed specialty meal, which will arrive in stores December 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas. McDonald’s is betting adults will want them with their meal, though. Instead of a plastic toy, the chain is offering free pairs of ugly Christmas socks with every purchase of its Home Alone-themed specialty meal, which will arrive in stores December 1. With each order, customers will get one of four pairs of festive socks featuring illustrations of McDonald’s characters like Grimace, or Macaulay Culkin’s Home Alone character, Kevin McCallister. [Photo: McDonald’s] McDonald’s isn’t alone in this. The socks, designed in the style of an ugly Christmas sweater, are kitschy collectibles that fit within the broader trend of apparel releases by food and quick service brands, and it’s bigger than ever this holiday season. Burger King and Wendy’s are also giving away cold weather gear —both happen to be beanies, and Burger King’s is Peanuts-themed—with their holiday meal deals this year, too. [Image: Burger King] Restaurants and food brands have turned to clothing and apparel in recent years to capitalize on “post-ironic” cultural relevance and to deepen brand affinity even as shoppers pull back on spending. Chains like Cava have released their own ingredient-themed apparel collections, while other brands have turned to unconventional partnerships, like PringlesCrocs or Hidden Valley Ranch-flavored chapstick. For some fans, restaurant merch has become the fresh band T-shirt. [Photo: Wendy’s] The happy-meal-toys-for-adults trend also comes as grown-ups are increasingly ordering kids meals, according to the market research firm Circana, which found adult orders of kids meals are up 28% since 2019. At Burger King, the No. 2 U.S. burger chain by sales behind McDonald’s, sales of its King Jr. meal are up 40% year over year, which the chain attributes in part to more adult purchases with no kids around. [Photo: Wendy’s] Designing a kids meal for adults, then, is catering to an already growing customer base. Instead of giving them toys with their meals, apparel is a giveaway that’s usable. Due to rising prices, customers have dined out less frequently over the past two years; to win them back, chains are focusing on quality and value. Though McDonald’s has fared better than many of its competitors, it unveiled a 0.2% decline in U.S. sales on its earnings call this month. To grow its domestic business, the chain is rolling out new menu items with smaller portion sizes and more protein, as well as leaning into specialty drinks and dirty sodas. Meals themed around nostalgic IP like Home Alone add up to another tactic. [Photo: McDonald’s] McDonald’s is marketing the meal as an invitation to “leave adulthood behind” by tapping into nostalgia, and letting the customers customize their meals by picking their own entrée. It also leans into Home Alone through its menu items: french fries rebranded as “Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries” for the film’s fictional pizza chain, along with a McFlurry, and pizza-flavored seasoning packet and dipping sauce. This is what a kids meal looks like when it’s “kidulting.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss.
  • Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter.
  • The pace stands out against the wider market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the manufacturer’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

The pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

The quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

For the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

In a recent development, all third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

Recent findings suggest that that makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

In the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

The second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the tech giant’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

Recent findings suggest that bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

— OGQ-Magazine (Online Gambling Quarterly) (@OGQMagazine) November 10, 2026.

CEO Robeson Reeves said development projects remain on track and market conditions are stable going into the fourth quarter and 2027. The Bronx casino resort is expected to cost $4.0 billion and open by 2030. Bally’s closed a financing package led by WhiteHawk Capital Partners that provided $400 million in term loans for the project. Another $160 million in delayed-draw commitments remains available. The term loans come due 18 months after they are first funded.

The delayed third-quarter 10-Q comes next. The firm has mentioned it should arrive before its five-day SEC grace period runs out.

Starbucks’ viral Bearista cup is back for the holidays. Here’s how they turned the cute cup into a collector frenzy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that starbucks obviously knows coffee, but the chain has also mastered the ability to sell endlessly collectible merchandise.
  • Industry observers note that starbucks obviously knows coffee, but the chain has also mastered the ability to sell endlessly collectible merchandise.
  • Recent findings suggest that in November 2025, the company introduced the Starbucks Bearista Glass Cold Cup in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that starbucks obviously knows coffee, but the chain has also mastered the ability to sell endlessly collectible merchandise. Collecting its mugs and cold cups has been a hobby of die-hard fans and online content creators who make videos about hunting for the latest drop, and interest in Starbucks merchandise reaches a fever pitch around the holidays. In November 2025, the company introduced the Starbucks Bearista Glass Cold Cup in the U.S. The handblown, bear-shaped glass cup for cold drinks came with a Starbucks-green beanie and a green-and-white striped straw that proved irresistible. Lines snaked around stores before their early-morning openings. More than one store witnessed physical fights, and videos on social media of people “hunting” the cup racked up views. The Bearista has been a recurring mascot for the brand since 1997, when Starbucks introduced a plush, green-aproned bear for the holidays. In 2023, it morphed into a cold cup in Korea, then spread throughout Asia before hitting the U.S. last November. By then it was already on cup collectors’ radars. Dana Pellicano, SVP of global product experience, Starbucks: We were seeing this trend of kidulting, adults leaning into playful, fun products. The confluence of that, [the bear’s legacy], and the rise of cold drinks made it the right time for us to bring it to the U.S. Carol Casey, aka RayahSunshine, cup collector/content creator: In the cup community, we see lots of cups coming out of other countries that are really enticing. We noticed that Starbucks Asia had a very unique set of cups. Their cups were more cutesy. The artisan quality of the cup meant its supply was very limited. That created demand for social media videos of how to find one, and even created a secondary market on eBay. In a statement, the company apologized to those who weren’t able to snag one. Pellicano: What makes it special is also what makes it logistically hard and part of the reason we had to be really disciplined about how we introduced it. When you say yes to something, you’re saying no to something else. So we are saying yes to this really premium, elevated offering and therefore unintentionally saying no to everybody being able to have one. These are the choices that you have to balance. Lindsay Ream, Starbucks coffeehouse leader, Grand Rapids, Michigan: Everybody wanted it. We get to the store at 4 a.m.—we open at 4:30—and when we got here, we had six cars in the parking lot waiting for us to open the doors. All day long the phone rang. We had someone answering all day to say “sorry, we’re sold out.” Casey: Because stores stagger their openings and resellers pop from store to store, it’s very competitive. I like to go where I know I can for sure get the cup. With the limited editions, you’re there at 3 a.m., and some people were getting there at 2. The Bearista bear went nuts. Everybody was trying to get it—and people were willing to spend $250 on eBay for it. It was so limited that it upset people more than not, but it did bring a lot of interest. Since last year, Starbucks has launched four more Bearista cups—the Pink Drink Bearista with a white hat and strawberry straw topper, an online-exclusive, soccer-themed Bearista for Starbucks Rewards Reserve tier members, and a Snoopy-shaped cup for fall. For the holiday season, the original Bearista is making a comeback, with a surprise box that contains one of four variations on the original, with the potential to include a rare golden Bearista.. Pellicano: We’ve really worked to refine our processes, and we’ve had a lot of success. We try to match the natural demand of where our stores see real volume in driving merch. We capped how many cups customers can purchase [at two per person]. Ream: In my district, we talked about partners not buying cups ahead of time. We have “partner access” where employees only were offered an early launch, but it didn’t come out of the amount of cups that we had for customers. Casey: I may hunt it [again] just for the sake of the hunt and the content—just because that’s what I do.

I voiced a character in ‘Grand Theft Auto.’ I never expected her to follow me for 17 years

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube.
  • The release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube.
  • Sources indicate that for me, as someone who works in digital editorial and audience engagement for a media manufacturer that covers tech and news, the data is staggering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube. For millennials who played video games growing up, this is a cultural moment. For me, as someone who works in digital editorial and audience engagement for a media manufacturer that covers tech and news, the data is staggering. It also reminds me of when I stumbled into the Grand Theft Auto universe in my twenties. In 2009, I was fresh out of Tisch School of the Arts at Newly introduced York University and was auditioning endlessly. I spent my days at castings surrounded by dozens of other girls who looked like me, only prettier. I spent my nights waitressing until the wee hours of the morning, or haphazardly attending parties and clubs where I admittedly hoped to be discovered. These were chaotic times: years of small successes, like a role on Law & Order or a bit part on a soap opera, separated by months upon months of fruitless auditions and absolutely no work. So when a friend from high school reached out to me about a gig recording voice-over for The Ballad of Gay Tony, a 2009 expansion of Grand Theft Auto IV, I swiftly accepted without asking many questions or seeing the script. To be frank, I wouldn’t have known what to ask about how the character interacted with the universe of GTA. My parents were strict, especially about video games. They were both educators and categorized video games as brain rot before that was even a thing, so I’d never played GTA before. I recorded Joni’s voice track in a couple of hours at Rockstar Games in SoHo, with my high school friend in the audio booth. This was the easiest acting job—there hadn’t been any awkward audition, all of my scenes were set in a nightclub, which was an environment I knew well, and I didn’t have to memorize anything. I just had a sheet of one-liners to deliver in a sassy club manager voice. Since I was a waitress at the time, I remember using one of my managers from The Coffee Shop on Union Square as inspiration. (I won’t name her out of respect.) [Screenshot: Rockstar Games] I needed to separate the character from myself because I wasn’t half as bold as Joni, who spent a lot of time propositioning Luis while simultaneously mocking his, er, body part size. It seems crucial to note that I didn’t realize players could interact with characters beyond speaking to them—in ways that are both violent and sexually violent—but I’m not sure I would’ve turned down the job even if I had known. After all, Joni was a character, she was just an avatar, and I was an actress. I left the studio with few regrets, and even fewer when the check cleared on time. This was 2009. The term “digital footprint” wasn’t part of the zeitgeist. Instagram didn’t exist, and I still typed websites I liked into my browser to check the news—and none of those sites covered gamer culture. Could I have anticipated that Grand Theft Auto would remain a cultural phenomenon that would follow me forever? I don’t think so. I also didn’t run in circles where “fandoms” were a thing, so I was surprised when fans of Joni started emailing me in 2010. In hindsight, this speaks to the growing popularity of the GTA franchise, and the fact that Joni was probably a lot of people’s cup of tea. Their emails were typically short and bizarre, and a few were desperate for a response. It takes a lot of deep thinking about a character to research the voice-over actor and email her, but if there’s one skill I already possessed at age 26, it was knowing that often no response is the best response. Not long after I recorded my voice-over for GTA, I began to suspect I had skills beyond acting. Motivated by the fact that I never felt particularly intrigued by the scripts I was given to audition for, I created my own web series, took a job managing social media and, through a combination of hard work and luck, very quickly built a media career. In 2011 or 2012, I took my acting website down and the emails stopped. When Instagram introduced direct messages, the messages returned, but at a slower pace. During the pandemic, I managed an editorial team that included a section dedicated to gaming. I’d all but forgotten about Joni, but decided to trot out my voice-over credit as a fun fact during one of those team meetings where we were all trying to bond as humans while working from home in isolation. When we finally returned to the office, one of the producers who’d been on the call brought me a poster of Joni as a gift. I unrolled it at my desk. There she was, a reminder of a period in my life when any job that was even moderately creative seemed preferable to serving mojitos. On the poster, Joni is happy as can be, spraying champagne into the air and grinning in her pink dress. It dawned on me that some of the people on my team had been teenagers when the game came out. I thanked the producer and tried not to imagine what sorts of interactions he might have had with Joni. I’ve managed to scrub much of my twenties from the internet—a feat I suspect only elder millennials will be able to pull off, as the internet grows more permanent and everyone becomes increasingly obsessed with saving “receipts.” But Joni is still out there. She occasionally resurfaces in my professional life, partly because Rockstar Games remains a cultural force, and partly because the way players interact with characters—especially women—is still a conversation worth having. I’ve spent years putting distance between myself and the person I was when I voiced her. Joni, meanwhile, is still in that pink dress, spraying champagne, having the time of her life.

#11756. Cities built 311—teachers need one, too

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1859 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Cities built 311—teachers need one, too

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach.
  • It has been revealed that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach.
  • In a phone interview with this article’s coauthor, Talia Milgrom-Elcott, Record described a student who loved science but whose severe dyslexia made chemistry, with its letters, numbers, and subscripts, a challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach. But last year, she ran up against the limits of her vast knowledge base when she stepped in to fill a vacancy and teach honors chemistry at her suburban high school in Stratford, CT. In a phone interview with this article’s coauthor, Talia Milgrom-Elcott, Record described a student who loved science but whose severe dyslexia made chemistry, with its letters, numbers, and subscripts, a challenge. Working with his parents and a special education coordinator, Record turned to the internet, YouTube, and AI for answers. She lacked the knowledge and tools to support him on her own, and because none of the other science or special education teachers had any expertise in this area, she had nowhere else to turn. As more AI tools and edtech platforms enter the scene, the marketplace of information teachers turn to for support has become more crowded and confusing, even for those working inside their areas of expertise. The abundance of available tools places the burden on teachers to determine which are effective, for which students, and under what circumstances, often with little guidance or support. LESSONS FROM LOCAL GOVERNMENT AND MEDICINE New York City had a version of this problem. Residents faced more than 40 agency call centers and no clear way to know which to call. In 2003, the city released 311, a single number for every non-emergency question, reachable by phone, text, app, or web. By 2022, it had received at least 500 million contacts, and cities around the world have copied it. Medicine has UpToDate, a clinical reference written and continually updated by more than 7,000 paid physician authors and reviewers. A doctor unsure of how to treat something gets a practical synthesis of the current evidence instead of a stack of raw studies. Both examples point to something education still lacks: a “Teacher 311.” This single go-to source would turn scattered expertise into clear answers that teachers can depend on. Building one would take rethinking and reinvesting in our nation’s education research infrastructure. HOW A TEACHER 311 COULD WORK A Teacher 311 could look like a texting-based hotline crossed with a living research engine. A teacher like Record could text or chat a question: How do I teach symbolic chemistry notation to a student with severe dyslexia? They would get back a specific, vetted answer instead of an unwieldy list of search results. Behind the scenes, master teachers, researchers, and school system leaders—paid for their expertise—would brainstorm suggestions and review AI-generated recommendations. They would set the standards for what the system would draw on: peer-reviewed research and educator-verified practices. Privacy protections would be built in from the start. As quality is proven and trust earned, AI could take on more of the first draft, but an expert would still review every answer. Teachers would rate responses, so the system improves with each question. The best answers to common questions would proactively go out to teacher networks and professional associations nationwide. Questions without ready answers would fuel the pipeline for education R&D those asked most often or with the highest potential impact on students would be prioritized. For years, the Institute of Education Sciences and U.S. Department of Education have been urging researchers to focus on “knowledge mobilization”: closing the gap between what research tells us and what reaches teachers and students. A Teacher 311 could be that bridge. WHAT’S NEEDED TO CREATE TEACHER 311 The idea for Teacher 311 came from Talia, who developed the concept and the plan to build it. Partnering with Alliance for Learning Innovation (ALI) made sense given its work on federal education R&D policy. ALI’s latest policy brief asks the federal government to build that infrastructure—the capacity to research and test ideas like Teacher 311 before they scale, so the ones that reach classrooms actually work. Senators Bennet (D-CO), Tillis (R-NC), and Van Hollen (D-MD) echoed that call in September when they reintroduced the New Essential Education Discoveries (NEED) Act. If passed, the bill would create the kind of agile center that could seed the investment to build and scale a project like Teacher 311. The federal government is well positioned to back something like this, and an administration that did could make it a signature service and a hallmark of its tenure. In the meantime, the private and philanthropic sectors have the opportunity to move the needle now. We estimate that the Teacher 311 hub would cost less than $5 million to build and $3 million per year to run, a fraction of the $2.55 billion the federal government allocated in fiscal year 2022 for education R&D (the year ALI conducted a funding analysis). Done right, the payoff would reach every level of the system. The Institute of Education Sciences and the National Science Foundation would gain a steady, practitioner-driven pipeline of research questions worth funding. States and districts would get better evidence on where to invest in professional learning. Most importantly, teachers would get useful, trusted guidance on the problems they’re facing, and their students would benefit. Teachers search for solutions every day to help their students. Record figured it out eventually, mostly on her own. The next teacher with a student like hers shouldn’t have to. Sara Schapiro is executive director of Alliance for Learning Innovation. Talia Milgrom-Elcott is cofounder and executive director of Beyond100K and Starfish Institute.

The energy strategy most companies don’t have

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades.
  • For trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades.
  • Global energy use keeps growing and electricity demand is rising more than twice as fast as energy use overall, according to the International Energy Agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades. Today it’s a competitive variable. Whether a business can secure the energy it needs—and afford it—increasingly determines whether it can grow. Global energy use keeps growing and electricity demand is rising more than twice as fast as energy use overall, according to the International Energy Agency. The problem is that war and geopolitical conflict, along with tariffs reshaping the cost of equipment, are affecting supply and cost. Policies are also shifting with election cycles. This year alone, oil swung from $118 a barrel to under $72 and back above $100, while Washington rewrote the nation’s fuel-economy rules. No single shock is decisive—the shocks compound. As a result, nearly every fleet and fuel-retail operator I speak with is wrestling with whether to use electric, diesel, or natural gas. However, energy markets are moving too fast and too unevenly for anyone to call it with confidence. The operators pulling ahead have stopped trying to choose one. Instead, they’re building the capability of running on more than one energy source—and deciding in real time which to use, where, and when. FedEx is a case in point. It now runs nearly 9,500 electric vehicles while testing renewable diesel for the long-haul trucks where, as the company puts it, “full electrification is not yet feasible at scale.” And it isn’t alone: Roughly 19% of North American fleets now operate EVs, and 30% run hybrid or alternative-fuel vehicles. PAY FOR FLEXIBILITY WHERE IT COUNTS Optionality isn’t free. A second energy source means added infrastructure, more complex procurement and, often, some loss of efficiency. No business can hedge everything. The discipline is deciding where flexibility is worth paying for. The most resilient operators I see ask two questions about every site, route, and asset: If this energy source were disrupted tomorrow, how much revenue would stop? And how exposed is it to a single fuel, supplier, or grid connection? Where both answers are high, redundancy is insurance worth buying now. A delivery depot that charges its entire fleet from one utility feed can’t run routes when that feed goes down. Where impact is high but exposure is modest, flexible supply contracts, rather than long-term agreements locking in a single source, may be enough. Where the impact is low, optimize for cost and move on. THE EASY PART IS THE HARDWARE Adding EV chargers to a forecourt or alternative-fuel trucks to a fleet is now easy. Running them together is not. A mixed-energy operation creates decisions a single-fuel business never faced. Which vehicle takes which route, given its charge level and the day’s energy prices? When should a depot charge its equipment to avoid peak demand costs? How do you compare cost per mile across diesel, natural gas, and electric when the data lives in separate systems? The advantage goes to businesses that can see their entire energy picture in one place and act on it. In a volatile market, the ability to switch is only as valuable as the ability to know when to switch. 3 MOVES WORTH MAKING NOW For leaders of fleet, fuel-retail, and other energy-intensive businesses, building a multi-energy operation starts with understanding where you’re vulnerable and what flexibility is worth. These three moves lay that groundwork. 1. Map your 24-hour exposure. Identify the sites, routes, and assets that would stop generating revenue within a day of losing their primary energy source. 2. Put a price on flexibility. Capital cases that compare only cost per gallon or per kilowatt-hour miss the value of being able to switch. Make the cost of downtime an explicit line in every energy investment. 3. Instrument before you diversify. You can’t coordinate what you can’t see. Bring fuel, charging, payments, and fleet data into a single view before adding the next energy source. Energy isn’t going to get more predictable. Leaders who build for adaptability will succeed whichever way it goes. As an executive, ask yourself: If your primary energy source were disrupted tomorrow, how rapidly could your business respond? Mark Morelli is president and CEO of Vontier.

Industry News: 5 leadership lessons the music industry taught me

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, spend enough time around live music and you rapidly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show.
  • Sources indicate that spend enough time around live music and you swiftly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve spent much of my career working in the music industry, from marketing and business development to managing independent venues and festivals, with stops along the way at Graceland, Fun Fun Fun Fest, DoStuff Media, and SXSW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spend enough time around live music and you rapidly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show. Behind every successful performance is an entire team of talented people working together to make awesome moments happen. I’ve spent much of my career working in the music industry, from marketing and business development to managing independent venues and festivals, with stops along the way at Graceland, Fun Fun Fun Fest, DoStuff Media, and SXSW. I’ve also spent plenty of time playing music myself, including a period when I was pretty convinced I’d be the next Dave Matthews. Today, as Huntsville, Alabama’s Music Officer, I’ve found that many lessons I learned working with artists, agents, promoters, production teams, business executives, interns, and others have been just as valuable in government as in the music business. Here are five leadership lessons the music industry taught me that apply to most professions. 1. IF YOU SAY YOU’RE GOING TO DO SOMETHING, DO IT. Reliability is a highly underrated leadership quality. One of the quickest ways to lose your team’s confidence is surprisingly simple: Tell someone you’re going to do something and then don’t follow through. The lead guitarist might have incredible talent, but if they’re consistently late and unprepared, the band probably won’t be enthusiastic about working with them. Whether it’s finishing a project, making an introduction, or getting someone the information they need to move forward, people rely on those commitments. Not delivering on responsibilities can throw everything off course. Trust is ultimately built through what’s delivered. 2. YOU DON’T NEED TO BE THE SMARTEST PERSON IN THE ROOM. Nobody has all the answers, and being in a leadership position doesn’t automatically make your ideas the best ones. Some of the most creative and effective solutions I’ve encountered came from people closest to the work. Think about everything involved in producing a concert. The sound engineer understands things about audio the promoter probably doesn’t. The lighting director has perfected their craft. The artist, stage manager, marketing team, and venue operators have their own areas of expertise. How much harder would that operation be if everyone had to defer to one person who believed they knew more than everybody else? Create an environment where people feel valued and empowered to speak up, challenge ideas, and suggest better ways of doing things. 3. SOMETIMES THE BEST LEADERS GET OUT OF THE WAY. Musicians, technicians, stagehands, managers, security staff, and ticket sellers have specific responsibilities. When everyone knows what they’re doing, the operation runs so smoothly that most in the audience don’t think about the work happening behind the scenes. Sometimes a well-intentioned person jumping in to “help” can make things harder. The same applies to leadership. If you’ve assembled a great team, trust people to do their jobs. Your team should know you’re there when they need resources or guidance, but there’s a fine line between supporting and micromanaging. 4. BE A CHAMELEON WITHOUT BEING FAKE. In music, I worked with artists, business executives, concert promoters, venue operators, and community organizations. In government, I’ve added elected officials, city departments, and other stakeholders to that mix. Each group has its own priorities and communication styles. Learn how to adapt to those environments without compromising who you are. Understand the room you’re walking into. What matters to and motivates the people you’re talking with? What do they need to understand to make a decision? There’s a distinction between adapting your communication and claiming expertise you don’t have. Don’t change your values based on who’s in the room and don’t underestimate how quickly talented, experienced people can recognize when someone isn’t being genuine. 5. EARN THE RIGHT TO TAKE BIGGER SWINGS. Making the transition into local government from a music industry career came with culture shock. The music business naturally rewards creativity, experimentation, and taking risks. Government, for good reason, places greater emphasis on process, accountability, and responsibly allocating public resources. Those two approaches don’t have to be mutually exclusive. Some of the most meaningful progress happens when you bring an entrepreneurial mindset into an environment not accustomed to doing things differently. The key is understanding that you must earn the trust to experiment. Plenty of people seem more interested in being viewed as innovative rather than doing the work necessary to make their ideas successful. Making a bold move to prove you’re a bold leader isn’t a good strategy. Instead, focus on building credibility through consistent execution, responsible decisions, and a track record of delivering results. Trust is organizational capital. When you follow through on a commitment, solve a problem, or demonstrate sound judgment, you build more of it. Eventually, that credibility allows you to propose bigger ideas and challenge conventional thinking. These calculated risks might otherwise struggle to gain support. When you do take big swings, be thoughtful about potential consequences. Make sure the people involved understand the vision, the risks, and what you’re trying to accomplish. The goal should be to build something meaningful that creates opportunities and continues delivering value years down the road. LEADERS: IT’S NOT ALL ABOUT YOU The most vital things I’ve learned about leadership came from working alongside talented people who knew how to get things done under pressure, and without much recognition. The best live performances are successful because people understand their roles, trust one another, communicate effectively, and take pride in contributing to something bigger than themselves. The same is true of great organizations. While the headliner gets applause, the entire team makes the show possible. Great leaders make sure everyone gets a standing ovation. Matt Mandrella is music officer of the City of Huntsville.

You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

  • You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

According to recent reports, instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.

In a recent development, text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a newly introduced one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

Recent findings suggest that …you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

In a recent development, email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

It has been revealed that you can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this latest Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when unveiled in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

#11749. 22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • In a recent development, accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • Sources indicate that we asked members of the Fast Manufacturer Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks. We asked members of the Fast Organization Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread. 1. TREAT MISSES AS INFORMATION Be as clear about expectations up front as you are about results afterward. Fear comes from ambiguity: People don’t know what success looks like until they’ve missed it. I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista 2. MODEL SELF-REFLECTION Accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. The more leaders model that kind of self-reflection, the more comfortable others will feel doing the same—and helping their teammates build that skill. — Grace Keith Rodriguez, Caliber Corporate Advisers 3. FOCUS ON LESSONS LEARNED Accountability should give people the confidence to take major swings. When it only shows up for the misses and mistakes, you create a culture of fear, which doesn’t inspire creativity or big thinking. Instead, be clear about expectations, set ambitious goals together, and when something falls short, focus on the lesson learned and move on. — Max Friedman, Givebutter 4. LEAD WITH CURIOSITY RATHER THAN BLAME Accountability without fear begins with clarity—clear expectations and realistic goals—balanced with my personal commitment to being accessible and providing timely feedback. This shared accountability builds trust as the same standards apply at both levels. When challenges arise, I am able to lead with curiosity rather than blame, asking “What happened, and what support do you need?” which creates space for my team to surface problems early and treat setbacks as learning opportunities. Consistency reinforces this sense of safety, so instead of fearing accountability, my team feels supported and invested in our shared success. — Maurice Twomey, Roto 5. ENSURE REAL ALIGNMENT FROM THE START Many tend to think of accountability as something you create at the end of a process. Someone didn’t do what they were supposed to do. Will you hold them accountable or not? In my experience, however, accountability issues are often alignment issues in disguise. What are we trying to do and why? By when? What are we both assuming? What is really feasible? Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process. They approach accountability not as a punishment question but as a clarity question—and in doing so, they debunk the idea that accountability and fear must come hand-in-hand. — Maril MacDonald, Gagen MacDonald 6. OWN THE OUTDATED DASHBOARD Accountability isn’t perfection. A team member flagged outdated targets on a dashboard I was presenting. I owned it and thanked them. Small moments like that set the tone for the big ones. When we miss a real target, we own our work and our choices and solve it as a team. Do that consistently, and you build that muscle for the harder moments. — Michele Walsh, UNICEF USA 7. SHIFT THE MINDSET When leaders shift their mindset from “don’t break this” to “let’s try this,” accountability becomes about outcomes and learning. As leaders, we need to role model what strong accountability looks like and acknowledge fear with grace and empathy. This means we should understand that some good ideas won’t stick, and we should celebrate innovative thinking even when it doesn’t result in a win. When people see their leader take a smart risk, own what follows, and adapt quickly, they do the same. — Jacqui Canney, ServiceNow 8. CUT THE ENDLESS APPROVAL CHAINS If you want real accountability, let team members own the outcome and cut the endless approval chains. Nobody likes to fail, but you can build a culture of permissible failure and actually walk the talk. When mistakes happen, address them head-on, take the lesson, and move on fast. — Khozema Shipchandler, Twilio 9. ASK WHAT HAPPENED, NOT WHO DID IT Make the destination crystal clear and the path flexible. Fear shows up when people don’t know what “good” looks like until they miss it. I’d rather over-communicate the outcome, agree on ownership out loud, and let people choose how they get there. When something goes sideways, my first question is “What happened?” not “Who did this?” Accountability is a promise teammates make to each other, not a punishment waiting to happen. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr 10. MAKE ACCOUNTABILITY A WEEKLY RHYTHM Accountability works when colleagues do the flagging, not the leader. Every week, especially in our executive meetings, we review our trackers top to bottom and call out anything blocked or at risk, in the open, in front of the team. It’s rare that someone gets blindsided in a one-on-one weeks later. Fear creeps in when accountability feels personal or arbitrary. A visible, weekly rhythm makes it structural instead, and that is what keeps people honest without making them defensive. Consistent communication is key. Beyond email and Slack, good ole phone calls and texts are quite effective. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will 11. TEACH CLEAN ESCALATION For our team, it all starts with providing clear communication so people understand what’s expected and how success will be measured. We approach conversations from a point of kindness and empathy, which includes listening and practicing radical candor so everyone is provided honest, respectful feedback and knows where they stand. Teaching clean escalation and other techniques also plays a role in maximizing accountability while preserving the best possible team dynamics. When people know they can raise issues early and get help addressing them, taking responsibility becomes much easier. — Leerom Segal, Klick Health 12. DON’T LEAVE PEOPLE GUESSING Clarity, transparency, and continuous communication. That is the foundation—and frankly, it is the ethos on which we built our company. When people know exactly what is expected, where they stand, and that honest feedback flows early and often, there is nothing to fear. Fear creeps in when people are left guessing. The goal is shared accountability. Not imposed from the top down but owned collectively by a team that feels genuinely empowered. When that culture exists, people hold each other to a higher standard because they want to—not because they have to. — Meredith Rosenberg, NU Advisory Partners 13. THE KIND OF FEAR MATTERS Fear isn’t always bad. Fearing your boss is different from fearing you didn’t do your best work. Top-down fear can produce compliance, but rarely excellence. I want my team accountable to themselves first, because people only do their best work on things they care about. That means clear quarterly and annual goals, professional development funds for growth areas, honest conversations about where they want to go, and a real grasp of why our work matters and why their contribution is key. People who hold themselves to a standard outperform people who only answer to a boss. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards 14. ATTACH A HUMAN OWNER TO AI-RELATED DECISIONS I would argue that it is the lack of accountability that creates fear. Accountability should remove ambiguity. Each artificial intelligence-related decision should have a human owner. There are clear rules of engagement that establish what is and is not in the bounds of permissibility. And when mistakes are made, they are inspected and not concealed. Fear breeds in darkness: Create light. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra 15. HAVE EMPLOYEES SET THE BAR FOR THEMSELVES Accountability is a matter of doing what you commit to. Our team members have some flexibility to set expectations regarding the timing and scope of their deliveries. Publicly demonstrating finished products in team or client meetings improves accountability. Fear is effectively removed when trying to clear bars we set for ourselves. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps 16. SHOW VULNERABILITY Model that it’s ok to own up to a mistake. We’re only human and no one is perfect. Ultimately that leads to greater accountability because there is an honesty at the heart of it. It removes the bullshit and gives folks the support they need to own their accomplishments, warts and all. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo 17. SET CLEAR EXPECTATIONS Every employee plays a role in the company’s overall success, but depending on their level or access to senior leadership, they may not see how their contributions impact the greater whole. What is important to the CEO? What are the growth ambitions of the company? How does each individual’s responsibilities ladder up to the organization’s goals? It is essential to set clear expectations for each person, provide honest feedback, and communicate transparently about how daily activities and individual performance are linked to company success. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners 18. WRITE IT DOWN Accountability holds when the measure is agreed before the work starts. Clarity is kindness, as they say. Set it together, write it down, and review it on a fixed schedule so a missed target shows up early and gets treated as information. People get defensive when the standard appears after the result, or when it shifts depending on who’s asking. Other than that, I try to give real guidelines and real feedback. If you start off that way, it instills the proper expectation of communication. — James Chester, WVN 19. DISCUSS HOW TO CLOSE THE PERFORMANCE-EXPECTATION GAP I try to set a high bar of excellence by sharing great work, and by praising and rewarding excellent work. That way, when someone isn’t delivering, we can point to the gap between their performance and the expectation and talk about how to close the gap. It’s designed to create a supportive, safe, and fair environment. No finger pointing and passive-aggressiveness allowed! — Phillip Haid, Public Inc. 20. TAKE AN ASPIRATIONAL APPROACH I’ve learned that empathy and accountability aren’t opposites. A few years ago, I leaned too far into being accommodating, and expectations slipped. I used to frame performance gaps as “We’re not where we need to be,” which I think created fear. Through coaching, I learned to take a more aspirational approach: “This is what excellence looks like. How can we get there?” It shifts the focus from fear to problem-solving. When people care deeply about the mission and understand what’s expected of them, accountability becomes a shared responsibility rather than something driven by fear. — Felicia Curcuru, Binti 21. REPLACE PUNITIVE REACTIONS WITH CURIOSITY AND COLLABORATION Having experienced the damage of fear-based leadership early in my career, I know criticism and punishment only breed toxicity and burnout. Accountability without fear starts with connecting our work to purpose. At a mission-based organization, holding ourselves accountable is directly tied to achieving our mission. When performance issues arise, leaders should replace punitive reactions with curiosity and collaboration. Approaching staff with two-way dialogue to uncover blockers, rather than one-way scrutiny, turns accountability into a partnership that helps everyone succeed. — Jaymes Black, The Trevor Project 22. SEPARATE THE PERSON FROM THE OUTCOME Accountability works best when expectations are clear before something goes wrong. I try to separate the person from the outcome, so the conversation becomes about what happened, what we learned, and what needs to change. Fear makes people hide problems. Clarity makes them easier to solve. — George Kailas, Prospero.ai.

In a recent development, accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks.

Sources indicate that we asked members of the Fast Manufacturer Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread.

I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista.

In a recent development, accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process.
