Tech Report: Anthropic stock is already falling today: Why AI giants are seeing a painful sell-off after record IPO

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Industry observers note that and today things are even worse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks. And today things are even worse. Nearly every major hardware manufacturer that makes components for the AI pipeline—from CPUs to GPUs to memory—is seeing significant share price declines. And then there’s Anthropic itself, the world’s most valuable pure-play AI firm. After a strong debut yesterday, its share price is down significantly this morning. Here’s what you need to know. What’s happening? In premarket trading this morning, the tech-heavy Nasdaq is seeing red, along with some of the largest AI players that trade there. As of this writing, Nasdaq futures are down nearly 1%. That’s after a significant fall of more than 550 points, or 2.25% yesterday. As of Thursday’s close, the Nasdaq was down around 5% for the week. Yesterday’s Nasdaq drop is all the more striking because it was also the day that Anthropic made its eagerly awaited market debut. The AI company’s IPO was priced at $83 per share, but those shares quickly popped to nearly $115 in early trading before ending the first day at $97.17—a 17% gain. Anthropic’s IPO was the largest in history, raising around $81.3 billion. The company’s market cap now sits at around $1.27 billion, making it the 12th most valuable company on the planet. Yet Anthropic’s success did little for the rest of the market. Throughout the day, tech stocks started falling, including those of other major AI players like Nvidia. This morning, Asian markets and major AI and tech players are down significantly. And on this side of the Pacific, the sell-off is continuing with major American AI-related stocks. As of the time of this writing, the following AI-adjacent stocks are down in premarket:  Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMD): down 6.5% NVIDIA Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): down 2.3% Intel Corporation (Nasdaq: INTC): down 5.2% Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down 4.8% SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 6.7% And yes, Anthropic’s stock price is down nearly 10%. Why are Anthropic’s shares sinking? Anthropic and hardware-related AI companies are both seeing their share prices sink in premarket trading, but maybe for different reasons. When it comes to AI hardware companies, those that make the components needed to power the massive server farms AI data centers require, there has been significant negative sentiment around them since at least October. Investors are increasingly getting uneasy with the major hyperscalers’ capex spending. Companies like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions to build out data centers, and most aren’t yet showing a clear path to monetizing AI enough to recoup those costs. If those companies cave to investor pressure and start scaling back their capex plans, it will hit AI hardware component makers (like Nvidia, Intel, and AMD) and memory makers (like Micron and SanDisk) pretty hard. Investors seem to be bracing for an inevitable capex pullback, which has weighed heavily on hardware-adjacent AI stocks recently. Other factors that have affected AI stocks lately include the Jensen Huang scandal and the ongoing fears that we are firmly in an AI bubble. But Anthropic doesn’t make hardware, and it just had its successful IPO only yesterday—so why are its shares down so much today? It likely has less to do with significant fears of capex spending and more to do with other factors. The primary factor is likely profit-taking. The company’s stock price rose more than 17% on its first day of trading. Many shareholders who aren’t bound by lockup periods are likely taking some of those profits this morning. Another factor—and one that could have significantly more long-term consequences—is that fears of an AI bubble and an AI slowdown are also likely weighing on investors’ minds. Anthropic has a massive valuation north of $1.2 trillion, but in the first nine months of 2026, the company generated only around $33 billion in revenue. Its net loss for the same period was $104 billion. Investors may be able to live with that discrepancy while the AI hype train is riding high, but enthusiasm only goes so far, and if the AI bubble bursts, Anthropic could be hit hard. Where do Anthropic shares go from here? That’s something everyone wants to know, and no one can tell you. The company’s share price has already fallen from its intraday debut high of nearly $115 per share to its current premarket price of $88.44. Contrast that with the company Anthropic just dethroned as having the largest IPO in history: SpaceX. When SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) went public in June, it was, until yesterday, the biggest IPO in history, raising $75 billion. Its IPO price was $135 per share, and the stock quickly jumped to more than $225 per share. But then it began falling. A month after its debut, SPCX shares were trading below their $135 IPO price as the hype wore off, and people began questioning the company’s future profitability. As of the time of this writing, SPCX shares are trading at just $131.66 in premarket trading. If ANT’s early life plays out the same way—and there’s no way to predict whether it will or won’t—the share price could be underwater for even IPO investors in just a few months. And if the AI bubble does burst, things could get even worse.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small upgrade to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.
  • According to recent reports, like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account.
  • These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small upgrade to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

According to recent reports, like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

Industry observers note that to launch, tap the new pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”.

According to recent reports, this is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now swiftly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

In a recent development, FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Check out 9to5Google on YouTube for more news:.

According to recent reports, editor-in-chief. Interested in the minutiae of Google and Alphabet. Tips/talk: abner@9to5g.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets. “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man mentioned at The Upcoming York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections. It’s easy to see why he feels that way, particularly in Texas, where Musk has moved his business operations and cultivated close ties with Republican leadership. Despite his extraordinary spending—$446 million, roughly half of which went to races in Texas—Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and swept the major statewide elections. That eye-popping figure includes $5 million for Republican incumbent Greg Abbott’s gubernatorial campaign and $10 million for Attorney General Ken Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid, both of which ended in defeat. But Musk may soon have much bigger financial headaches than any futile campaign contributions. The incoming Democratic administration in Austin could complicate the billionaire’s plans to expand his sprawling business empire. Indeed, Texas’s governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has already signaled that she intends to be less accommodating of the kinds of tax breaks and land deals that helped lure Musk to the Lone Star State in the first place. Abbott has by contrast been an enthusiastic champion of Musk’s Texas vision, appearing alongside him at firm events and celebrating his investments in the state. Abbott and Musk reportedly keep in close contact, and the governor’s office even fought to prevent the release of months of communications with the tech mogul’s companies, arguing that they contain “information that is intimate and embarrassing and not of legitimate concern to the public.” With Hinojosa in office, Musk can no longer count on that same level of intimacy, though he did offer a more sanguine assessment of his future in a blue Texas at the DealBook conference, predicting that Hinojosa would govern as a moderate. “I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said. Billions in tax breaks Musk’s companies have to date been given the royal treatment from the state. SpaceX, for instance, scored roughly $1.66 billion in potential property tax breaks for its planned Terafab semiconductor facility in Grimes County, between College Station and Houston, according to the Houston Chronicle. The incentives, approved by two local school districts under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program, could cut the company’s school property taxes in half for 10 years per phase of construction. SpaceX also secured a $30 million grant from the Texas Enterprise Fund. Hinojosa has made no secret of her disdain for such arrangements. “I do think we should wipe clean corporate welfare in this state,” she told the Texas Standard in October, singling out Musk’s billion-dollar-plus tax break. She’s also pushing to reveal to the public more about Musk’s relationship with Abbott. In October, she sued Abbott for access to unredacted emails involving Musk and his companies. But Hinojosa won’t have an easy time undoing those incentives. She would have considerable discretion over the Texas Enterprise Fund, although recovering money already awarded would depend on the grant’s terms. Reversing the much larger property tax breaks would prove far more difficult. Those agreements are made among the company, local school districts, and the governor, who cannot simply terminate them over a change in policy. State law does allow the governor to revoke the incentives if a company fails to meet certain employment or wage requirements, but even then, the company must be given an opportunity to remedy or challenge the violation. To that end, Hinojosa has said she plans on reviewing Musk’s existing incentives to ensure his companies are meeting employment obligations. Those requirements can be remarkably lenient: Per the Chronicle, SpaceX needs to create just 80 jobs at its Terafab facility to meet the minimum employment threshold for the school-district tax incentives. SpaceX’s South Texas expansion Hinojosa’s victory could also throw a wrench into SpaceX’s expansion plans in South Texas, where the company is pursuing massive new infrastructure projects—and seeking additional land for its operations. For starters, there’s the $24 billion data center and natural gas-fired power plant planned near its Starbase headquarters near the border with Mexico. SpaceX confirmed the project earlier this month and notes construction activity has already created more than 3,000 jobs, though the facility is not yet operational. (That project has already encountered resistance from local officials, with Cameron County commissioners voting this week 3–2 against advancing SpaceX’s request for a 10-year, 100% property-tax abatement for the project.) Hinojosa has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center approvals until Texas lawmakers enact stronger protections for water supplies, electricity customers, and surrounding communities. And she’s also indicated that projects already underway wouldn’t necessarily be exempt: “If it needs a permit that the state has to approve, then that’s on hold,” she told the Chronicle last week. Again, though, SpaceX has gotten a head start. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality this week approved an air permit for a natural gas plant associated with the project. But that permit covers only the power-generating component, not the entire $24 billion development. So Hinojosa could still hold up the project if SpaceX needs additional state approvals once she takes office. Meanwhile, SpaceX has also been pursuing a deal to acquire state-owned parkland near its Boca Chica launch facility, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. Texas Monthly reported last month that state officials were considering selling 1,300 acres to the company, raising obvious questions around coastal access and habitat preservation. Hinojosa, who grew up in nearby Brownsville, asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department shortly after her election to hold off on any action during the transition. SpaceX has since clarified that it wants approximately 1,200 acres of public parkland surrounding its launch facility—not Boca Chica Beach itself—and says it would preserve half the property as coastal habitat. And SpaceX could face another headache at Boca Chica. Benjamin Flores, the Democrat who is the incoming Texas land commissioner, plans to challenge a 2013 law allowing temporary beach closures for rocket releases, Texas Monthly reports. And while the state Supreme Court threw out a previous challenge in June, that rejection came on procedural grounds, leaving the law’s constitutionality unresolved. A possible Tesla–SpaceX merger Tesla and SpaceX have been discussing a merger, which would bring Musk’s EV, rocket, satellite and AI businesses under one corporate roof. The state’s new Democratic leadership could throw a wrench into those plans. Texas’s incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already signaled that he intends to take a very close look at any such tie-up. “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny,” he told Bloomberg last week, citing concerns about corporate concentration. Johnson’s office could investigate potential antitrust violations and, if deemed warranted, challenge the merger in court. Unlike Hinojosa’s proposed data center restrictions, which could require new legislation or regulations, that authority already exists under state law.|.

#11744. Peeping AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy,’ notes Meredith Whittaker, so Signal is blocking screenshots

Peeping AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy,’ notes Meredith Whittaker, so Signal is blocking screenshots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.
  • AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.
  • Sources indicate that signal is the latest platform to make changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions. Signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices. “An existential threat’ Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, unveiled the change in a blog post. Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.” The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Customers can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee. Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work. Signal is fed up with a lack of AI assistant transparency The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” indicates Whittaker. She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.”  The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data. She further stated that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility. Whittaker issues a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”.

AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.

Sources indicate that signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices.

Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, confirmed the change in a blog post.

Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”.

The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Customers can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee.

Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work.

The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” says Whittaker.

She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.”.

The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data.

She further noted that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility.

Whittaker issues a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”.

  • A leaked screenshot reveals further information on the Custom Cards feature under Samsung’s Now Brief umbrella (via SamMobile).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we know Galaxy AI subscriptions are coming soon, but the details have been kept under wraps. A newly introduced leak says Now Brief’s custom cards are the next targeted feature to be adjusted, even though it was assumed only new features would require a subscription.

When Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI plan leaked, only a couple of details were made public. For starters, the plan will reportedly cost $5/month and add latest features like Bixy Action, Daily Briefing, and Gen Video. Those new features would require a paid subscription, but existing ones would be left alone, right?

It’s a bit of both, apparently. A leaked screenshot reveals further information on the Custom Cards feature under Samsung’s Now Brief umbrella (via SamMobile). For the time being, Custom Cards are limited to three. The screenshot demonstrates Galaxy AI Premium will allow consumers to create and edit more.

Custom Cards act as a sort of task for the Galaxy AI model, making it possible for users to set up complex widgets that appear in Now Brief. That ranges from weather to health information for very specific use cases. It’s a tailored widget – useful, but far from groundbreaking.

But even with the upped Custom Card limit, Samsung’s Galaxy AI Premium subscription doesn’t appear to equate to “unlimited.” The screengrab claims this:.

Creating and editing cards uses Al Plan credits. You can only create and edit cards if you have enough credits remaining.

Credits are shared across devices signed in to your Samsung account.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy AI Premium plan will let customers buy “credit packs” on top of the $5/month subscription if they run out. It’s unclear how many credits Custom Card creation eats up.

Technically, this falls under “new feature,” since Custom Cards have long been limited. Still, it would have been nice if Samsung expanded the ability as Galaxy AI has improved in lockstep with other models.

Sources indicate that we don’t know what the majority of Galaxy AI Premium looks like beyond these few details, but we likely will soon. In any case, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been an excellent device for those of us who hardly use Galaxy AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: fresh concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She’s pretty sure she’s not the only one.“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having … I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.It’s an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days’ tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it’s a familiar one, too.Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it’s one they’re likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.” Air travel is vital — and taken for granted In some ways, the country’s aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy … and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.“You’ve got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There’s nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she’s used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she’s not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure challenges to the list of potential problems, she’s not rattled by it.“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to “Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something,” she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?” The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can’t just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking manufacturer Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter’s flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She’s keeping the rolls in her garage“The funny part,” she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.” AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story. —Deepti Hajela, Associated Press.

According to recent reports, at this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: upcoming concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her prepares to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She’s pretty sure she’s not the only one.“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having … I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” stated Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.It’s an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days’ tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it’s a familiar one, too.Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it’s one they’re likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”.

In some ways, the country’s aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy … and frankly, it is taken for granted,” noted Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.“You’ve got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There’s nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she’s used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she’s not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure concerns to the list of potential problems, she’s not rattled by it.“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to “Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something,” she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”.

According to recent reports, if anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can’t just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking manufacturer Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter’s flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.The upfront cost was worth it, she stated, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She’s keeping the rolls in her garage“The funny part,” she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”.

AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

—Deepti Hajela, Associated Press.

‘Worst COP ever’? Climate talks in Turkey are near the finish line and activists are in an uproar

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators fighting over how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change.
  • climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators fighting over how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change.
  • Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year’s U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators fighting over how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding.Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, mentioned they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday. Worries about a ‘worst COP ever’ Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year’s disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding.If fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa.In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.“The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.”In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.“There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!” As climate talks near their end, fossil fuel debate rages One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.But the final draft doesn’t spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push.“At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa.The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change.Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text’s draft.“We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey’s Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said.“Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere,” said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.” Vulnerable nations say climate finance is lacking Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don’t emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change.They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need.The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft’s previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually.Many of the world’s most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year’s talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.It’s richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it’s hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room.Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker.“Disappointment is rife,” said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.“Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said. Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report. The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Industry observers note that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that proposal. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

It has been revealed that bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Sources indicate that medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the firm states you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Recent findings suggest that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

It has been revealed that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that stepping back in time a few days, Anthropic last week launched Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The frontier model races continues. A week after the launch of Anthropic’s Claude 5.2 and Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol as a “new standard for professional work.”.

Industry observers note that stepping back in time a few days, Anthropic last week launched Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2. The company’s latest models are “designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges with “improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision.” Anthropic states that Fable 5.2 beats Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Carbon virtually across the board in benchmarks including coding, cybersecurity, knowledge work, and more.

But, now, OpenAI is stepping up to the challenge.

OpenAI shows that GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are more or less playing ball with Anthropic’s latest models, but often delivering similar performance at a drastically lower cost.

Of the two upcoming models, OpenAI indicates that Sol is “smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan” as a “go-to model for everyday work.”.

Astra, meanwhile, is tuned for the highest-quality work in professional use cases such as documents, slides, coding, and more:.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a fresh quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu people in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Astra being significantly more affordable compared to GPT-6 Astra. Pricing for Astra per million tokens lands at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. Sol matches its predecessor at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output, again per million tokens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

According to recent reports, spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

According to recent reports, “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta enhancement, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp consumers.

Google Home is constantly rolling out fresh updates and, today, the manufacturer is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to users.

Industry observers note that the first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone.

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:.

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and new keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six fresh countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”.

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

It has been revealed that the first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat people in the US and Canada that demonstrates “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

Industry observers note that A third enhancement is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “Fresh” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

According to recent reports, dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out newly introduced Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that weekly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest patch from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

In a recent development, today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

Sources indicate that for most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows promptly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

Sources indicate that the damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

According to recent reports, nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

It has been revealed that automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

Sources indicate that look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

Industry observers note that what closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

It has been revealed that here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

Breaking: YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (409 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.
  • Sources indicate that view counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays.
  • Now, YouTube claims it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

Sources indicate that view counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube claims it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

In a recent development, in a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube says it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

Industry observers note that how is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

YouTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

This change is rolling out now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

According to recent reports, motorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

Across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

In a recent development, MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

The October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

It has been revealed that greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

The citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

Retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

MotorCity also led the sportsbook results. It posted $928,607 in retail receipts. MGM followed at $746,215, with Hollywood Casino at Greektown close behind at $729,350.

Industry observers note that the sportsbook activity generated $90,878 in state taxes. The casinos also sent $111,073 in sports wagering taxes to Detroit.

The city’s take from the casinos goes well beyond sports betting. In October, Detroit collected $13.4 million from the three properties, combining its share of gaming taxes with sums owed under each casino’s agreement with the city.

Sources indicate that the “catch” is that you’ll still need a subscription to use this. Gemini Live has always required a subscription on Google Home speakers and smart displays, with the functionality looped into Google Home Premium prepares which start at $10/month (or bundled into Google One AI Pro). #11712. Latest Update: Tokenomics In Commercial Real Estate AI: 4 Questions To Ask Before Starting Each Task

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Tokenomics In Commercial Real Estate AI: 4 Questions To Ask Before Starting Each Task

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snow, Co-Founder and President of Ascendix Technologies.
  • ​For many firms, AI cost management begins with an unexpected bill.
  • For a long time, the cost of each AI task was hard to track, partly because the tools didn’t show it and partly because there is no clear understanding of how many tokens each task will take.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wesley D. Snow, Co-Founder and President of Ascendix Technologies. 30+ years in software development; a pioneer in AI for Real Estate.

​For many firms, AI cost management begins with an unexpected bill.

For a long time, the cost of each AI task was hard to track, partly because the tools didn’t show it and partly because there is no clear understanding of how many tokens each task will take.

As a solo worker who uses AI for tasks it can facilitate, and not every little thing in my to-dos, I rarely hit the token wall. But as the head of a manufacturer full of workers who are curious about exploring AI and implementing it into their workflows, an overcharge is actually something I expect.

In a recent development, AI companies priced their intends to win market share, and many consumers, including me, built daily habits around those tools. The next invoice is often an unpleasant reality check. Mine was $1,500, and it came from a single automated job. ​.

According to recent reports, ​AI providers bill each request in tokens, and a token is roughly three-quarters of a word. Each request is billed for what AI reads (cheaper input tokens) and, separately, for what it writes (more expensive output tokens). For example, according to Anthropic’s current pricing, Fable 5.1 charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens it writes. So, each written word costs five times as much as a read one.

It has been revealed that the choice of model is an even larger factor than the read/write price split. The smallest Claude model, Haiku 5.5, charges $0.10 per million input tokens, 100 times less than Fable. By my rough math, a typical deal summary costs about 15 cents on the top model and less than a penny on the smallest one.

A difference of a few cents matters little for one request and adds up quickly for automated jobs that run many times a day. ​​.

Sources indicate that looking up a contact or sorting emails by sender takes a person a few seconds. An AI assistant, given the same task, searches your connected systems and reads through records to find a phone number you could have looked up yourself, and you pay for every record it reads.

Summarizing a 60-page lease or rebuilding a deal history from scattered emails takes a person’s hours, and AI does it in minutes, so the time saved easily covers the token cost.

Because output tokens cost more than input ones, tasks with a lot of reading and a short answer are the cheapest way to use AI.

It has been revealed that A lease summary fits that pattern, since the AI reads the full lease and writes a page or less. An interactive dashboard or a deck works the other way, because nearly every token in it is generated output. Generating an email is still relatively cheap, especially when you do not use the most advanced model on such a trivial task.

Visual, dynamic, interactive and self-updating output is the most expensive kind.

A mistake in a rough first draft of an email takes a minute to fix, while a lease abstract with the wrong rent escalation can lead to a billing dispute and a lost client.

Recent findings suggest that AI tools make errors more often than their confident tone suggests. Invented details and outdated information are not as common in AI output as it used to be, but the time spent checking should count toward the task cost.

A question you ask once is billed once, while a job that runs on a schedule is billed on every run for as long as it stays switched on.

Recent findings suggest that my $1,500 bill came from a scheduled job. A while back, I set up a job that reads my inbox every three hours, matches senders to CRM records, and logs the emails. It reads every message, including unqualified cold pitches from data sellers and follow-ups from a webinar I attended once. It ran on the most expensive model because that was the default setting, and once it was running, I stopped checking it. ​.

Large companies run into the same problem on a larger scale. Uber reportedly used up its 2026 AI budget in four months and then capped employees at $1,500 per tool per month, roughly the amount my inbox job cost me. ​​.

Run a week of your tasks through those four questions and sort them into the ones worth sending to AI and the rest.

Lease summaries, meeting prep from emails and notes scattered across systems, deal histories and first drafts can usually be sent to AI, because each one replaces hours of reading with a short answer that is quick to check.

Contact lookups, inbox sorting and dashboards nobody opens can usually be done without AI, because a person can do them faster or nobody uses the result.

Repeating this as your tasks, the available models and their prices change will lead you to effective AI cost management instead of slowing down AI adoption or stopping its use at all. ​.

It has been revealed that it also helps to tell the AI that you’re working within a budget and ask it to flag tasks where a cheaper model or a shorter answer would do. In my experience, it suggests useful savings once it knows that cost matters. ​.

It has been revealed that I still use AI every day, but I now check what a task will cost before I hand it over. The inbox job behind my $1,500 bill has been replaced by an AI email parser built for that task. It operates on a cheaper model and can process every incoming email automatically, but I keep that setting switched off and send it only the emails I want logged in the CRM, so webinar follow-ups and cold pitches never reach it.

#11709. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1698 w)
